The House resumed, from Monday, October 21, consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Landry (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to resume debate on Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, introduced by my hon. colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald).
Mr. Speaker, in the first part of my speech, I explained why our Government introduced this legislation, and I subsequently elaborated on the conditions for implementing its provisions. I also explained at that time why our Government had not imposed quotas.
I had started to say that as of 1988, employers affected by this legislation will be obliged to file a report in respect of the immediately preceding calendar year, containing the following information:
First, the industrial sectors in which employees of the employer are employed, the location of the employer and employees, the number of all employees of the employer and the number of persons in designated groups so employed;
Second, the occupational groups of the employer and the degree of representation of persons in designated groups in each occupational group;
Third, the salary ranges of employees and the degree of representation of persons in designated groups in each range and prescribed sub-division thereof; and finally,
The number of employees hired, promoted and terminated and the degree of representation in those numbers of persons in designated groups.
Employers who fail to comply with this obligation will be liable to a fine not exceeding $50,000.
Employment Equity
On the basis of the detailed information provided by employers, the Canadian Human Rights Commission will be able to hear complaints it receives and conduct certain inquiries.
Since we wanted this legislation to be as flexible as possible, we decided not to impose enforcement mechanisms.
Mr. Speaker, in the opinion of this Government, setting up an enforcement agency would generate very high administrative costs. Moreover, it will be perceived by many employers as undue interference by the state in their personnel management policies.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that our Government has made a formal commitment to reducing administrative red tape, which more often than not tends to curb productivity.
Instead of an enforcement agency, our Government has opted for the even more redoubtable mechanism of public opinion.
As of June 1, 1988, all employers affected by this legislation will be obliged to file annual reports. The conclusions of these reports will be consolidated by the Department of Employment and Immigration and subsequently tabled in Parliament.
On the basis of the information contained in these annual reports, it will be possible to measure progress in the area of employment equity. The public will be invited to look at the results. Employers who fail to observe the equity principle will be clearly identified, and under the pressure of public opinion, they will be forced to change their personnel management policies so as to provide more jobs for the four groups designated in the Bill.
A number of my opposition colleagues feel that this surveillance mechanism does not go far enough, and that the pressure of public opinion is not strong enough to improve the conditions encountered by women, native peoples, visible minorities and the handicapped on the labour market.
I would remind these critics that public opinion is the most formidable tool we have for changing the behaviour of Canadian employers. Let us not forget the successful campaign organized by Canadian women in 1981 to urge the Government to include women's rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that Bill C-62 will affect more than 750,000 employees. In conjunction with other Government programs designed to stimulate labour market participation, Bill C-62 is a giant step forward towards social equity. From now on, the groups concerned by this legislation will be able to take their rightful place in Canadian society.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore urge my hon. colleagues to refer this Bill to the Legislative Committee as soon as possible.

They have been strong for 30 years and then they have developed a bad back problem or some other physical ailment which prevented them from being able to perform the type of work which they had performed for so many years. Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to rise in my place to participate in the debate on Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity.
It must be said from the outset that I do not think there is a Member in the House who disagrees with the fundamental principle or purpose of what is to be attained by this piece of legislation, or any other legislation which we may be considering in the coming weeks, months and years ahead. 1 am speaking of the fundamental principle that every Canadian in this country ought to receive equality of opportunity in the workplace, that is not a fancy right. It is not a privilege. It is a basic, human and fundamental right.
The Bill before us has four target groups, namely, women, native people, the disabled and visible minorities. 1 would like to preface my remarks with respect to the latter group since our critic, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) has indicated in broad terms how our Party views this Bill and has left it to a number of individual critics to look at the independent categories or target groups.
One has to look at this Bill, Mr. Speaker, and agree that the principle or purpose is good. Yet the follow through, the action taken to attain that principle, is far from perfect. It moves simply too slowly and is too weak in the ways proposed to attain employment equity for Canadians in all regions of the country. It is weak in the face of some landmark reports which this Parliament has recently received such as the Equality Now report and the Abella Commission report. I quote from the report of the Abella Commission which stated that "a Government genuinely committed to equality in the workplace will use law to accomplish it and therefore give the concept credibility and integrity."
1 do not think this piece of legislation gives credibility and integrity to that principle. Underlying the Abella Commission Report are two key focal points or concepts: mandatory and tough equity programs and the enforcement mechanism whereby those equity programs would be carried out. There is an absence in Bill C-62 of both those concepts. As Judge Abella stated in her report, "Unenforceable rights are no more satisfactory than unavailable right", and I think that speaks volumes to this piece of legislation. It is not a mandatory and tough equity program. It is a Bill which qualifies the program, is open-ended and not rigid, and does not set forth criteria with respect to'Government Departments, Crown corporations and companies doing business with the Government. It is not a mandatory program. Both the Abella Commission Report and the Equity Now Report suggested in very firm terms that voluntary and open-ended programs have not worked in the past, they have not attained the type of results which we, as a Parliament and as a country, should be aiming for.
I am quite surprised that the Hon. Member who spoke before me suggested that it is in public opinion and in voluntary programs taht we attain the best results. That is false. In certain instances which I will be outlining in my speech later on, public opinion is very lacking. We have to impose some sort of leadership and direction in a mandatory program so that equality in the workplace can in fact become a reality. We cannot leave it to the whims of the people involved. A mandatory program is the only route to go.
There is no enforcement mechanism specifically stated in the Bill. The Minister and Hon. Members on the Government
October 23, 1985

side have mentioned that the Human Rights Commission will be taking a look at enforcing the employment equity legislation. There are two things wrong with that. First, it is not indicated in any firm way in the Bill itself. There is no mention of the Canadian Human Rights Commission in the legislation. It was only indicatetd in passing. It was only dumped on to the commission in an informal and very loose kind of way. Second, and most important, is it fair and is it within the jurisdiction of the Canadian Human Rights Commission to do the kind of watchdog surveillance which this Government is imposing upon it? The Human Rights Commission, as we all know, is trapped for resources with respect to personnel and finances as it is. We all know that the Human Rights Commission is a reactionary body. It reacts on a one-on-one, a case-by-case basis. If we are talking about a national employment equity program which is going to ensure and guarantee that Canadians receive the equality which should be theirs, I feel it would be unfair to expect the commission to undertake this kind of enforcement mechanism.
There is a need for the Human Rights Commission. It is a body which is doing good work. But with respect to a national employment equity program, we need an enforcement body which will be somehow independent, active, full-time, and with enough staff who are qualified and familiar with labour relations, the employment system and human rights issues in general.
With respect to the voluntary nature of the legislation, the Minister in a press release announcing this Bill stated, and I quote:
The employment practices and policies of federally regulated businesses will go on public record, and these companies will have to answer to the people of Canada if they fail to achieve equity in employment.
Quite simply, Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough. If we are to look at public opinion and voluntary action, we also have to look at a number of recent reports from Toronto with respect to the whole question of racism in the workplace. The report entitled "Who Gets the Work?", which was published in January-a study commissioned through federal funding and conducted by the Urban Alliance on Race Relations and the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto- outlined some very serious concerns. It spoke forcefully against letting public opinion and voluntary mechanisms do the job for us. The author of the report said that "while whites were treated courteously, blacks applying for the same jobs were treated rudely, discourteously and with hostility." The report found that "in direct approaches on 36 jobs, white applicants received 27 offers and black applicants only nine." The report concluded "that the most significant amount of discrimination was directed at Indo-Pakistanis who were told that jobs were closed and no longer available in nearly 44 per cent of the cases." The report also indicated that "the black West Indians were told that jobs were closed to them in 36 per cent of the cases".
In the follow-up to that report, in May of 1985, it was found "that only 9 per cent of 200 large companies stated a firm belief in racial equality. Twenty-eight per cent of the employ-
Employment Equity
ers said they felt non-whites in general do not have the ability to meet job performance criteria compared with whites. Another 13 per cent saw non-whites as threatening, particularly if non-whites gained promotion over whites. Seven per cent expressed outright contempt for non-whites and 3 per cent viewed non-whites as a group to be justifiably exploited for low wages and long work hours."
I am not suggesting that those views reflect the views of all Canadians. But if we are to allow voluntary mechanisms, and the public will, to decide these matters, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, that we will fail. We will fail as a Parliament and as a nation to address and correct some inequality and some wrongs which are happening in the workplace to ordinary Canadians. This Bill has failed to address those concerns in a very real and concrete manner.
There is no mention in the legislation about contract compliance. There is nothing in the legislation which says that any company doing business with this Government must submit to some stringent employment equity measures. Only several months ago, we had a perfect example of this when I repeatedly raised on the floor of the House of Commons instances of outright discrimination which were being encountered by Canadians of Haitian and black backgrounds in the taxi industry, particularly in Montreal, Toronto and Hamilton. That was a perfect example of where this Government could have put its foot down and addressed the issue of equality which should be everyone's right, by sending a clear and strong message to the taxi industry that if it is to do business at our federal airports, then the industry must reflect the equality which should be every Canadian's right. Yet this Government shied away. The former Minister for Multiculturalism, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) shied away from setting this example, which reflects the same philosophy this Bill reflects. That is, we are not doing enough. It would have been easy to have told those cab companies that they are not permitted to do business at our airports unless they clean up their act and provide equality for all their drivers regardless of colour or background. The Government could have done that but it did not.
When we talk about contract compliance, we can look to our neighbours down south. Sometimes we say that we as a nation are much better than they are regarding human rights. Yet it is interesting to note a report submitted by the Canadian Ethnocultural Council which made some very interesting observations about the United States concerning contract compliance. They said that in the U.S. contract compliance legislation exists under Order 11246 which requires that federal contractors and federally-assisted contractors implement affirmative action programs. This applies to contractors with 50 or more employees and contracts valued at $50,000 or more. The program must set significant, measurable and attainable goals for the hiring, training and promotion of minorities and women. The numerical goals and timetables are directed towards increasing the utilization of target group members.

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity
Violation of the contract's equal opportunity clause may result in the cancellation or termination of the contract.
What have been the results? In 1983, the U.S. Department of Labour released the results of a study of some 77,000 factories, offices and work sites representing in excess of 20 millions employees. Between 1974 and 1980 minority employment grew at a rate of 20 per cent among those companies holding federal contracts, compared with only 12 per cent for businesses not bound by contract compliance. In addition, minority workers also posted significantly greater upward mobility where affirmative action was enforced. Finally, large numbers of blacks and Hispanic peoples moved from service and low skilled blue-collar work to skilled production, craft and white-collar jobs.
That is a perfect example of contract compliance being used to improve the economic lot of American citizens who had faced discrimination for a number of years. We could have done the same thing. Yet there is no mention of contract compliance in this Bill. There is no mention of that leadership I was talking about regarding the cab industry. However, that is what the Bill should have been speaking to.
I reiterate, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of this Bill is completely welcome in this House. There is not one Member who would disagree with it. However, it is the follow-through and the lack of real teeth in the Bill which lets down the target groups the Government is saying it is trying to help. If we are to increase the equality of these four target groups and other Canadians, as an Hon. Member mentioned previously, we need to have legislation which will not only speak to equality but which will deliver equality.
In a study conducted this year, Mr. Speaker, Canadians from visible minority groups represented only 1.7 per cent of all employees within the federal Public Service. This Bill does not speak to that. There has been some mention of programs being introduced by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) but they, too, are statistics gathering, research and study oriented. Yet what Canadians from one coast to the other are calling for are some measures which will deliver equality and tear down that vertical mosaic which still exists and which says that only a select few might be able to make it to the top. Other Canadians, through no fault of their own and not because they are incompetent, have been unable to reach the roof-tops which other Canadians have reached. That is a shame.
We can also look at what other groups are saying about this Bill. The Urban Alliance on Race Relations says "that the focus of the legislation is on data collection rather than hiring and training in a workplace free of discrimination." The Canadian Ethnocultural Council said that "while it is encouraging to see movement towards employment equity, the present Bill appears rather anaemic. It is difficult to envision how a voluntary approach will substantially improve employment opportunities for visible minorities."
Those words, as well as the meetings I have had with a number of groups and individuals, reflect how Canadians at large have accepted this Bill. We have also had a large number
of women and disabled and handicapped groups saying the very same thing. Their wish and my wish and the wish of my Party is that the Government listen attentively to these descriptions of the shortcomings of this Bill. The Government has a huge majority and we all know it can push through any Bill it likes on any day of the week. So what we should be concerned about is passing legislation which will do what it is intended to do. In my opinion this Bill does not do that. There should be employment equity for all Canadians. It is not a privilege, it is a right. It is a necessary part of being a Canadian living in a tolerant society. We all know there are people out there who, through no fault of their own, are not being treated with equality in the way that perhaps you and I are. This Bill needs to be improved. It needs amendments. It needs to speak forcefully and boldly to employment equity, and not just go through the motions. We need to have mandatory equity programs in our Civil Service, Crown corporations and those companies doing business with the federal Government. There should be no qualification regarding the number of employees or the amount of business concerned. What difference does it make if you do $100,000 or $2 million of business with the Government of Canada? Equality must transcend the financial and political barriers we see being created in this Bill.
In closing, I would like to caution the Government and the Minister to beef up this Bill with amendments which will ensure that these four target groups, and any others as was suggested earlier, receive the employment equity which is theirs by right as Canadians. I urge the Government to take another look at Bill C-62 because it will not improve the lot of these four target groups quickly enough or well enough.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments. The Hon. the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mrs. Landry).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to clear up a few points and maybe respond to some of the objections raised by my colleague from York West (Mr. Marchi).
I would like to point out to him that compliance with Bill C-62 will be mandatory, not optional. That being so, the companies will have no choice but to abide by the legislation.
The other point I might clear up has to do with frequent references to the enforcement mechanism and the Abella report. I would like to stress that we fully endorse the Abella report, particularly with respect to the enforcement mechanism. The Abella report mentions four models and we are in favour of the fourth one since it relates to the Canadian Human Rights Commission. In that sense, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that we too are endorsing the Abella report recommendations.
October 23, 1985

The last argument regarding the enforcement mechanism is that the Government has decided not to set up another costly agency, which would only add to the existing bureaucracy. We suggest that the data contained in the reports submitted by the businesses will make it possible for the Human Rights Commission to take legal action. And we believe that this enforcement mechanism will meet adequately the requirements of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, in her previous speech the Member said that an enforcement mechanism and a mandatory program would be too cost prohibitive. I think that is what is wrong with this Bill and with the mind-set of the Government. It is putting dollar figures before fundamental human rights in the workplace.
The Member mentions that companies have to report. They do. It mentions that in the Bill. The Government says that each company that does not file a report will be fined up to $50,000. That is great, too, but why not fine the companies if they are not fulfilling the proper equity programs which the Government has not really outlined to start with? If the Government is prepared to fine them for lack of reporting, it seems to me somewhat silly not to fine the companies for failing to attain a certain figure as established by the Government. That is the wrong way of doing things, Mr. Speaker. If you are serious about ensuring that employment equity will be a reality in this country, you must show direction and criteria and you must have some targets. If we are going to lift the four target groups up to an even level, we need to provide direction and targets and be specific.
I, too, Mr. Speaker, am against quotas because in themselves they impose limitations. However, we need more than just words. We need a criterion that companies can follow in order to attain employment equity. It is not good enough to say simply that if you do not file a report you are going to be fined. You should be fined and lose the contract if you do not attain employment equity aside from reporting to the Government with a letter or a report. Any company could submit a nice letter or report, but how can the Government judge whether that is in fact happening when there is not an enforcement agency on a national scale which can assure us that those reports are legitimate and reflect the reality in that company?
Those are the things which the Hon. Member should be addressing in addition to looking simply at what the Bill contains. It contains a number of positive elements, but it moves too slowly, is too weak, and there is no real courage and guts underlying the Bill because it is rather soft.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) who has just spoken. I feel he has made a good speech. I wish, however, to ask him a question, for he seems to be quite familiar with this issue. He seems bent on telling the Government what to do. He seems to be saying to the Government: Go ahead! Give more teeth to the legislation for a number of reason which he has enumerated. My question is quite simply
Employment Equity
this: As you seem to think that this bill should have more teeth, how long ago, in your opinion, should it have been implemented?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the Hon. Member. I do not pretend to have all the answers or to speak with the authority of anyone else except that of a normal Member of Parliament doing his or her work. 1 am disappointed that every time a piece of legislation comes up, Hon. Members always look back to what happened five years ago or twenty years ago when the Liberal Government was in power. That argument can be used for the positive things that were done in this country, yet no one does that.
However, I am not prepared to get into that kind of debate, because I do not think it speaks to this Bill. That kind of debate, discussion and rhetoric does not speak to the four target groups; women, natives, the handicapped and visible minorities. When we have a Bill intended specifically for those four target groups, we should focus debate on how we can get a piece of legislation which is going to work through the House of Commons, on how we can improve the piece of legislation to the best of our ability, and how we can further improve the piece of legislation through liaison with the four target groups and other groups that parliamentarians may be meeting with.
That is the kind of discussion that we should be having and that is the kind of discussion that Canadians are expecting from the parliamentarians in this Chamber. That is what I was trying to do. I was trying to look at this piece of legislation rather than looking 20 years in the past. Rather than looking to the past, let us try to envision what will be happening 20 years in the future. Let us ask ourselves where these for target groups will be in five years because of this legislation. If the answer is that they will not be far ahead, we should have the courage and integrity to ensure that employment equity will be insured. However, I honestly do not feel that it will be achieved through this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Member on his speech about the four target groups and what we should be doing in this country in terms of equity and equality. My question is very simple. Where was the Liberal Party for the last 20 years?

Mr. Speaker, I throw the question back and ask where the Hon. Member was two minutes ago when I was attempting to remove the partisanship with regard to this Bill. I think this is one of those Bills which should transcend the partisan nature which my hon. friend from Saskatchewan injects into the debate.
This Bill needs improving. It needs more teeth. I am prepared to stand in my place and suggest that the Government make those improvements. I am also prepared to say that if the improvements are made in the Bill, when it comes time to vote I would not be a hypocrite, just because I am on the other side, and not vote for it.

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity
We should recognize a good piece of legislation, but we should also be prepared to have the courage to recognize bad legislation.
[Translation\

Mr. Speaker, I strongly support this bill respecting employment equity, the purpose of which is to ensure equal rights within the labour force, so that nobody can be deprived of employment or promotion opportunities for reasons other than his or her qualifications. It especially aims at correcting the wrongs suffered by women, the natives, the handicapped and the visible minorities.
Employment equity requires not only equal treatment for everybody but also special initiatives and arrangements aimed at specific groups.
My political credo can be summed up as, "Fair shares for all and special privileges for no one". This Bill on employment equity addressed the first part of that credo "Fair shares for all". Employment constitutes a key area in which the right to equality and the equal benefit of the law must be achieved. Employment is one way for Canadians to become fully contributing, independent members of society. Employment equity is a way of eliminating discrimination against some Canadians in the employment area.
Let me quote from the report of Judge Rosalie Abella on which most of the legislation before us is based. I note that in her words:
Employment equity is a strategy designed to obliterate the present and the residual effects of discrimination and to open equitably the competition for employment opportunities to those arbitrarily excluded. It requires a special blend of what is necessary, what is fair and what is workable.
I can think of no Minister of the Crown or member of the federal Government better able to bring legislation before this Paliament that combines those three goals-a special blend of what is necessary, what is fair and what is workable-than the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald).
I want to say much about this Bill. However, to begin on a personal level, I want to say for the record that I have had the pleasure of knowing the Hon. Minister since the 1960s. The discussion we have had on the role of Government and the importance of Canadians realizing their potential and overcoming the obstacles that face them, including the obstacles of discrimination in the workplace, are not new ideas to her. Although the Abella Report provides a great basis for this legislation, this was not an idea that occurred to our Minister for the first time on reading the Abella Report.
The Bill before us now is the outgrowth of a long and serious commitment to seeing that Canadians enjoy their fair share. I want to salute the Minister for bringing this legislation before the House and enabling Canadians to see again that they have a Government in office now that not only is prepared to listen
but prepared to act and redress some of the long accumulating inequities in Canadian society.
In the few moments available to me, 1 want to base my remarks on this legislation in the context of four areas. They are the historical context, the constitutional context, the parliamentary context and the philosophic context.
Let me begin with the historical context. This legislation clearly constitutes a special program to see that women, the handicapped, the visible minorities and native Canadians have greater access to jobs in the Canadian economy. However, it is not the first time that Parliament has seen fit to make a special effort to see that social justice is done and that equity is more than a glib expression, that it becomes a reality.
Let me cite two examples. The first example is the veterans legislation that was enacted at the conclusion of World War II. The purpose of that legislation was to give special advantage, frankly, to the men and women who had gone abroad to fight for and defend this nation and indeed preserve the freedom that we are enjoying in Parliament and across the country today. It was felt that those who had put their lives at risk for our defence and liberty certainly should get more than just a warm handshake on their return to this country. Therefore, special programs were put in place with respect to educational opportunities and housing for veterans.
In slightly more recent times we have seen a special program to redress the imbalance in a country with two major founding cultures. It was a program to redress an imbalance in the federal civil service and to see to it that over a period of approximately a decade Canadians whose first language is French have higher and more important positions in the federal service. Those are two examples of how Parliament has seen fit in the past to move where social justice demanded it.
We now have a third spcecial program, and it is the Bill before us today.
Let us turn to the constitutional context. I will simply note in passing that Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees the legal equality of all Canadians and prohibits discrimination. Some might suggest that features of this legislation will be discriminatory in their effect. It is important to understand that Section 15(2) of the Charter anticipated that Parliament, on certain occasions, would have to redress historic imbalances and that special programs, such as this employment equity Bill, would be required. For that reason, in adopting the Charter several years ago, Parliament provided express exemptions, stating that programs aimed at ameliorating the conditions of those who had suffered past discrimination would not be unconstitutional under Section 15.
The third area is the parliamentary context. By that I am referring to all the other companion activities and legislation coming through this Chamber as part of the great outpouring of our Government's response to the long developing inequities in Canadian society. While the employment equity Bill is an important piece of legislation, it does not stand alone as the sole response of the Government to these problems. Contemporaneously with this we have passed amendments to the Indian
October 23, 1985

Act, thereby removing over a century of discrimination against Indian women.
In another development a few weeks ago, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) announced in the House a Charter litigation fund to ensure that Canadians who want and need to challenge existing laws and programs, because they are not constitutional under our new Charter of Rights and Freedoms, would not be precluded from doing so because of a lack of financial ability. Indeed, a few months ago, in the same parliamentary context, Bill C-27 went through Parliament. It was an early initiative of the Hon. Minister of Justice to eliminate a number of the obvious inequities in existing federal statutes in light of the equality provisions of Section 15 of the Charter. Bill C-62 is but a companion piece of legislation in an over-all attempt by the Government to fulfil its commitment to social justice in Canada which was one of the three goals that were enunciated in the Throne Speech as a hallmark of our Government.
That brings me to the fourth context in which I would like to consider this employment equity Bill-the philosophic context. This is the context in which I speak about the merit system or about meritocracy. I believe that the ideal system is the one in wjiich people are hired and promoted on the basis of their merit. You write the job description setting out the bona fide requirements for whatever the task might be, a transportation shipper, a gunner in an aircraft, a lawyer, a bus driver, and then you hire the person most qualified. That is what I call meritocracy.
In a country such as ours, with people from so many different national backgrounds, different religions, walks of life and political belief, you really cannot have any other system. What we want to see is the very best for our country. We want Canada to realize its full potential by having individuals realize their full potential. Let us not see discrimination against anyone. Let us see only hiring of the best. That is the ideal. We must always keep that in mind. Even when special programs are brought in, such as in this Bill, it is not to detract from that ideal but to work closer toward it.
As a Conservative, I believe philosophically that human institutions reflect the human frailties that we ourselves possess and that it is not a perfect world. I accept that the old boy network operates when people are hired and promoted. I remember and take to heart the expression often heard when people are being hired for jobs that it is not what you know but who you know that counts. It is in that context that we see this legislation introduce a concept that can redress and do some fine tuning in the working of meritocracy. It is unquestionably the case that native Canadians, disabled Canadians and visible minorities have not had their fair share of jobs.
I would like now to address some of the specific reasons that I think this is a good Bill and, in many respects, an historic breakthrough. Let us consider first the gathering of data.
I have heard and listened with careful attention to spokesmen for the Opposition Parties being critical of the reporting
Employment Equity
requirements. I thought I was perhaps hearing comments that could have been made by people who escaped from the Titanic as it was going down who found themselves in a lifeboat and who were criticizing the lifeboat. You have to take it step by step and view the value of what we are doing on its own merit. There can be no question that the compiling of data is fundamental to the evaluation of not only why this legislation should be brought in but of how well it is achieving its goal. When it has achieved its goal, we can revert to the working of the meritocracy system without any of these special programs. Until we have the data lines and the information that can say, yes, a fair share is now being won by those who, in the past received the butt end in Canadian society, a lot of the debate and discussion is more rhetoric than genuine concern for seeing true human progress.
I should note that some of those who have criticized this legislation feel it is not the desire, the will, the interest or the wont of the corporations, the business community, to see special programs that would encourage women, the handicapped or other disadvantaged groups to get a fair share of the jobs.
It was, therefore, revealing to me to have had a number of conversations recently with corporate executives, particularly those responsible for personnel policy, men in their fifties in most cases, who are speaking with a new-found glee, the kind of enthusiasm that comes to a born-again reformer part way through life on discovering that something formerly being opposed was not only positive but did not hurt. By recruiting women, formerly having excluded them, they found far better, more motivated people coming to companies and doing a much better job. I do not want to generalize on the basis of perhaps half a dozen or more conversations, but I put that before the House as a straw in the wind. There is an increasing recognition that things are changing on the part of those who once opposed or just dug in their heels on the basis of stereotypical notions of who should be doing what, where and under what circumstances.
We spoke a year and a few months ago that it was time for a change. That message has gone deep not only with the Government of the country but in the way we are thinking, in the way we can reform and introduce new programs, such as the program contemplated by this employment equity Bill, to see that all Canadians get their fair share.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) has, in the course of his comments in praise of the Government Bill before us, suggested that institutions reflect the imperfections of humanity. This is one of the more interesting dodges that Conservatives use for their own slow action.
Is it not a necessity for institutions to seek to transcend the imperfections of humanity? Is it not the responsibility of Government, recognizing the shortcomings in employment equity that exist, to get on with the task actively and not give us half-baked measures of the sort we are debating in Bill C-62?

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's comment and question has two parts to it. One having to do with the speed with which our Government is responding. The second is a more interesting philosophic question. First, on the question of speed, I do not think anybody on this side of the House has to apologize for speed. Has the Hon. Member counted the number of days from the time the Abella Report came out to the time that the legislation came into this House? Compare that with the record of any Government, including provincial Governments and New Democratic Governments, and Members will see that the Progressive Conservative Government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration do not have to apologize to anyone in terms of getting on with social justice. I always love to hear from the New Democrats when it comes to seeing someone other than a New Democrat doing something that is for the good of the people, because they feel that that area is their own private, protected preserve. We Progressive Conservatives are here because the Canadian people know that they can look for us for action, and they are getting it.
Hear, hear!

The second point in his question had to do with the philosophic nature of human imperfection and whether institutions reflect that or not. I think this is perhaps long going to be a point of discussion between socialists and members of the Progressive Conservative Party. My view is that human nature is flawed, that we are not perfect on this earth and therefore our creations reflect that, be they reports that are written, be it legislation that is introduced, be they speeches given by Members in the House. No matter what we turn to, we can always think later how it might have been better. When 1 am talking about institutions reflecting human imperfection it is not because I do not think they can be improved. I think that is the continuing struggle that particularly we in politics are engaged in, to pursue that endless quest to find the golden mean. But if the Hon. Member thinks that in one single Bill perfection can be achieved, then I suggest that he remain in the New Democratic caucus. For our part we are going to stay on this side of the House and support the Minister of Employment and Immigration who is bringing in legislation that is a special blend of what is necessary, what is fair and what is workable.

While my friend is waxing eloquent over there, in his capacity not only as a Member of this House but, I gather, as chairman of the subcommittee on equality, he is talking about the imperfection of institutions and so on and how great this particular Bill is in terms of the four targeted groups. I wonder if he would be prepared to entertain the idea perhaps of recommending to the Government that we extend equality to this institution and perhaps have an equal number of men and women Members of Parliament, have two-member ridings where there must be at least one woman and one man, therefore we would have gender equality in the House of Commons. The Minister said she would come and run in
Yorkton-Melville. We would then of course have two very excellent Members from that riding, as she is such a red Tory.
I wonder if the Hon. Member would comment on that. I do not make the suggestion in a frivolous way. Also I know our native people have said many times that perhaps we should look at the possibility of direct elections to the House of Commons of the native people of Canada. They represent such and such a percentage of the population. They are unique people with a distinct and special status in this country. What about the possibility of direct elections so that they could come here and represent native people?
What about those two ideas in terms of promoting equality in this country? I understand, Mr. Speaker, it is a bit of a departure, but second reading is debate on principle.

Nobody is perfect.
Dealing with the two points, I have already explained what 1 believe very strongly is important in Canada, namely, a system of merit, a meritocracy. I apply that not only to the job market or to other institutions but indeed to this very special institution, our Parliament. I think that those who are elected here should be elected on the basis of their merit, what they stand for, what they are prepared to stand for, their Party's record and what the Party stands for.
I would like to note for the record that, based on merit, we are getting an increasing number of women Members of Parliament in this Chamber. I would hate to see any kind of quota or artifical system introduced in our election procedures that would say that the people who come here are not the 282 who fought the hardest and fought the best and did the best they humanly knew how to, to come here and represent the people. I would not want anyone, including the Hon. Member, to think that he was here simply because he was filling a quota and not because his electors saw him to be eminently qualified to represent them.
As to his second point, it is interesting that one other country has tried that, and I refer to New Zealand, where they have the four Maori seats in their Parliament. In addition to all the other MPs, there are four who are elected to represent the Maori population. That system of course requires voters to register as either Maori or non-Maori voters, and then they have the choice of voting in one of those four Maori constituencies or indeed in the regular constituencies.
What has struck me as being somewhat anomalous in that is that it really gives the Maoris a bit of a special advantage because they know that they are going to get their four Maori seats anyway, so in the other seats they would probably vote for the candidates who would most likely be supporting and advancing the cause of the Maoris. I do not have any problem with that, but I just say that I think it introduces an anomalous feature into the electoral system. There are Maoris being elected in New Zealand through other than the four Maori constituencies, and I think that they are viewing this in New Zealand now as being the historic phase in which they find themselves now and that perhaps the time has come to end that artificial provision in their elections and to revert to a
October 23, 1985

system such as we have here. With regard to the New Zealand experience, I do not know that it would be an improvement here. I certainly can think of native Canadians who have been in this Chamber as well as in the upper House and who are here now and are contributing in a very fine fashion. They are here on their own merit as well.

The Hon. Member uses the arguement of merit, and of course that is always the argument, between affirmative action and merit. I guess we could go on at great length as to why we need some affirmative action programs. Accepting what he says about merit, is it not so that the Conservative Party has in its constitution for conventions, certainly at different levels, a parity principle whereby a certain number of delegates must be women at a leadership convention or a national convention of the Party must be women. It is certainly the case in our Party. Relating to our national council of the Party, we now have a parity provision whereby there must be an equal number of males and females.
I guess my question is very simply then, if we accept the concept of parity through affirmative action within our Parties: What is the difference when it comes to this institution, in terms of the Hon. Member's argument?

That is a good question. I would add that there is indeed a third dimension within the constitution that you could call affirmative action, special treatment, because there is a requirement that there be a certain number of youth delegates as well. Just before I answer the question let me say that I wonder if the Hon. Member was studying the Progressive Conservative constitution so intently perhaps at one time recently when he was thinking that this Party was doing so well that he would look at the constitution to see what if anything prevented him from joining this Party.
Even he is welcome.
We keep a light in the window for everyone.
I would never get elected.

Strange things happen and strange things happen in terms of Party constitutions as well. I think that, historically, that would have been a strange thing in terms of any Party's constitution. I am glad the Hon. Member raised it because it brings into sharp relief the importance of having, at different stages in our evolution as a country, programs that will help offset the workings of a system that, by any objective criterion, are not really fair to the over-all community. I think that is perhaps the one shared basis of philosophical agreement between socialists and Progressive Conservatives, our overriding concern for the community.
That, of course, goes back to where we both come from, from the 19th century, tracing back our philosophical origins and realizing the overriding concern for the well-being of the community in ensuring that there are no groups, be they women, be they youth, be they visible minorities or any other groups, that are being excluded on the basis of prejudice or discrimination. There is then clearly a role for the Government
Employment Equity
to step in, as we are doing now in this legislation, just as political Parties have stepped in in terms of those constitutional amendments or provisions that the Hon. Member so properly referred to in this context.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is now over. Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate Bill C-62 with a deep sense of disappointment which has been expressed by various groups and many Canadians when they have contemplated this Bill. The Bill is described as an Act respecting employment equity. In Clause 2 of this quite short Bill, the purpose of the Act is stated as follows:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the work place so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfilment of that goal, to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the same way but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences.
This Bill is part of an historic evolution of the employment practices of this country which calls for the action of Government. The Bill points us to developments which have taken place over the preceding years in opening up employment possibilities for women, and the federal Government has played its part in that, in creating federal and provincial programs to sensitize employers to the potential that exists in persons with disabilities, in creating programs which are designed to open employment possibilities for aboriginal peoples and in opening up employment opportunities for persons who are members of visible minority groups. I am particularly concerned with the last area to which I referred as I am the NDP critic for multiculturalism.
In the case of visible minorities in which I am particularly involved, the last Parliament saw significant developments in the form of a special committee which dealt with the participation of visible minority groups in Canadian society and also saw the Government of the day appoint a commissioner to consider the question of employment possibilities for members of that group as well as for members of the other three groups with which the Act deals. One could take time to explore the ways in which Canadian society has been sensitized somewhat to the problems of members of each of these four groups. Governments have come to recognize that it is necessary to develop legislation to ensure that progress can be made.
It seems to me that the present Conservative Government has now an historic opportunity to ensure that there will be real action taken to achieve equity in employment. I submit that Bill C-62 is a deeply disappointing piece of legislation in its approach to that goal. At best, one would have to say that the Bill is a truncated piece of legislation. At best, it is the first part of what the Government should have put before us.
The Bill could be defended if it were made clear that the Government planned within months to follow through on other

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity
actions that are required in order to ensure that there will be real progress made toward equity in employment. However, there has not been any real indication of that.
Since the Bill before us is supposedly complete in itself, we are waiting for the next Government to come in, as reporting will have to take place over several years before problems become clear, and only at that point will the next Government, in its wisdom, spend months deciding what should be done and creating the mechanisms that have been called for. Perhaps I concede too much in suggesting that several years will be required.
I would like to put before the House this afternoon the facts of the situation as they are spotlighted in Canada's largest city, namely, Toronto. Toronto is not an unusual city for these purposes. Its society reflects the nature of Canada in many ways. Employment practices which were found to exist in the City of Toronto as they relate to members of visible minority groups can surely provide us with adequate reason to think that the Government should take strong action.
I am focusing particularly on the report of the Urban Alliance on Racee Relations and the Social Planning Council of Metro Toronto which was published earlier this year under the title No Discrimination Here? This report indicates that a survey of personnel managers of 199 Metro Toronto organizations suggested that employers are doing very little about racial discrimination in that city. The large majority of Toronto employers have no policies to prevent discrimination or promote employment equity. They do not want such policies and claim that they are unneeded. However, the study concludes that race-related policies are indeed needed. Widespread use of informal personnel systems provides ample opportunity for exercising racial bias and unfortunately racial bias is often expressed by key decision-makers.
Some remarkable facts were elicited by the authors of this study in their consideration of how employers discriminate against non-whites in the Toronto labour force. There were in fact significant opportunities for discrimination, particularly in recruitment. There was a high degree of informality in the recruitment systems, and a correlation between the use of these informal practices by the employers and low representation of non-whites can be made.
Eighty-two per cent of the employers studied had no special policies to address race-related employment issues. Those who did have a policy, most commonly depended on a passive approach which was expressed in a statement of compliance with the Ontario Human Rights Commission guidelines. Only 3 per cent of this group of almost 200 organizations had developed systematic affirmative action plans at a time when surely the activities of Human Rights Commissions would have demonstrated the need in Canada for organized action if there is to be a real change in pattern.
Among the evidence of this unfortunate situation that the report put before the Canadian public was the fact that many employers overlooked or discounted the existence of interracial tensions in their workforces. On the one hand, there were complaints from whites in which derogatory race-based generalizations about work habits, hygiene and the like were being made. These were clearly expressions of how people felt in an aesthetic sense. On the other hand, complaints of non-whites focused on racially discriminatory employment decisions and practices ands race-based harassment in the workplace. One of the most remarkable statistics that came out of this study was the evidence that half of those non-whites who complained about these procedures ended up suffering from the fact that they had complained by being disciplined in some way or other. In such circumstances, it is obvious why employers do not want affirmative action guidelines developed.
It is clear that the reporting provision contained in this Bill will not make employers' lives very difficult. They will in fact be able to go on with the imperfections that exist, as the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) suggested a few moments ago, because they are not required to do anything beyond reporting on the situation that exists in their workplaces.
These features of the employment situation facing persons from visible minority groups in the City of Toronto would, I think, be matched across the country as well as would the features of the employment situation facing other target groups with which this legislation purports to deal and for which I would suggest it provides no effective means to ensure that progress will actually be made. I dare say it is no secret to any Member who has looked into the matter by now, and the Conservative Members will make brave speeches in support of the legislation, that various groups which have considered the legislation have found it quite inadequate. The study from which I have been drawing was sponsored by the Urban Alliance on Race Relations. The alliance has made its criticisms quite clear with respect to the equity in employment Bill. There are a number of shortcomings which the Bill fails to address.
First, what is missing in the legislation is a central enforcement and standard-setting agency for all four sectors, that is, Government departments, federally-chartered Crown corporations, contractors who do business with the Government and federally-regulated businesses. In fact, there is a very real possibility that the lack of any central enforcement agency will lead to various organizations or businesses falling under the sway of one or other of several different agencies. Our expectation is that the Canadian Human Rights Commission will have the primary responsibility. However, there is a possibility that other agencies, too, will become involved in this matter. As several agencies become active with various groups of employers, it is quite possible that different standards will develop. All we need is that type of additional inequity to open opportunities for lawyers to involve themselves and for judicial actions to begin which will further encumber the progress which so badly needs to be made in the country.
If there is one central failing in the Bill it is the failure to establish any central mechanism with adequate resources to the task. If there is any fundamental reason for asserting that
October 23, 1985

the Government blew it with respect to this particular Bill and that it in fact spoke brave words but refused to bite the bullet, refusing to rise to the challenge and get on with the job of moving toward equity in employment, it is in the failure to establish an agency which would have the responsibility for ensuring that real progress is made. It is not just a central and independent agency that is required. What is also called for is mandatory programs for the four sectors of employment to which I have already alluded. What is needed are mandatory programs which will ensure that progress is made by the four target groups with which we are concerned. Again, pursuant to this legislation, employers will be required to report. However, the hope that reporting, even publicly, will make any significant difference is an old-fashioned, small "1" liberal hope. I would have thought that the Conservatives, who know about human imperfection, would have seen this through and realized that they had to do much more than just ensure that information came in. Given the imperfection of humanity, what is required of employers if we are to have real employment equity is the establishment of plans, the setting of goals and the establishment of time-frames within which progress has to be made. It is by such means that this Government could have demonstrated that it was really prepared to do something about it and that it was prepared to act in areas in which it states its principles so bravely.
As far as contract compliance is concerned, which is one of the provisions by which Government can affect employment patterns in businesses which hope to sell to Government, what we need is contract compliance for all Government contractors with over 50 employees and $200,000 worth of Government contracts per year, not just undefined commitments as a condition of tendering. That is surely part of the same process of ensuring that enforceable plans are developed and that goals are set. With the figures in place, the possibility exists for the enforcement agency, which is imperative, to ensure that we are really seeing some progress made.
One of the basic principles which should underlie these new contractual arrangements is the provision that equal pay should be the basis for work or should result from work of equal value. There, too, this Bill fails in what has been one of the key concerns of all who are in support of the improvement of the economic position of women in our workforce.
Finally, as one other criticism which the Urban Alliance on Race Relations stated as far as this Bill is concerned, there is not an employment equity program requirement as a condition of all loans, grants and receipts of cost-sharing moneys. These several failings which the alliance raises with respect to a number of specific points were also expressed by the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, a national umbrella organization which is becoming more and more well known in the way in which it brings together various ethnocultural groups in the country and speaks for them nationally.
The Canadian Ethnocultural Council filed an extensive response to issues in equality rights with the subcommittee which was looking into the matter of equality rights over the summer and into the early fall. In its extensive report in
Employment Equity
commenting on Judge Abella's employment equity report specifically it said that a review of the United States experience with mandatory affirmative action confirmed the commission's view that legislated enforceable requirements are critical to the success of affirmative action programs. It also said that the commission concluded that the enforcement of employment equity requires an agency which is independent and which has a qualified staff familiar with labour relations, employment systems and human rights issues. If that is the requirement, what does this employment equity Bill do? The council suggests that the Bill is rather anaemic and that it does not provide any enforcement component in the area of contract compliance. There is little to ensure the contractor's commitment to equity programs. There is a lack of any enforcement mechanism. There is also an absence of guidelines to promote participation by visible minorities.
Those points underscore what the Urban Alliance on Race Relations said for its part as far as the shortcomings of the Bill are concerned. The fact of the matter is Governments, when they are determined, can make real progress. There can be no doubt in anyone's mind considering the Public Service of Canada that the 1969 passage of the Official Languages Act and the establishment of the Commissioner of Official Languages and a joint committee to oversee the matter led to action. Of course, there can be no doubt that the Government of the day lead by Prime Minister Trudeau was determined to see the institutions of this country become bilingual. As a member of the joint committee 1 am keenly aware of the shortcomings which still exist in the actual operations of Government and the existence of French as a language of work in Government. For example, in various areas of the country Canadians still find it difficult to be served in the language of their choice. All that after a decade and a half of determined action.
In these other areas legislation dealing with employment equity, pulling its punches the way this one does and failing to establish the mechanisms which are required of various sorts in order to make employment equity a result, can only leave one convinced that this Government is not really serious about the matter. It will talk about the matter but it will not take the action which is required to transform our society. It leaves all of those who watch convinced that society will not change very significantly. Certainly, if it is to change it will only be slowly. As I suggested when I spoke on The Nation's Business last Wednesday morning, it is that conviction held by so many Canadians that in time everything will be fine which I want to challenge. In fact, it requires the real determination of Government. This Government has not in fact followed through in a convincing way in demonstrating that it intends to do something, that it wants society to be changed in accordance with the principles of full involvement. I think we are all involved, including every Conservative Member of Parliament, in the kind of betrayal of principle by a Government which had the challenge in its hands and failed to do anything, which reflects very ill on the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). Each time the reports came out in

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity
Toronto last winter and spring, I wrote to express my very real concern about what Government could do, but the Minister has in fact failed to follow through-and I am sorry she is not in the Elouse to hear me say that-and that is cause for the deepest disappointment and a real sense of betrayal.

Mr. Speaker, I do not believe any of us in this House of whatever Party would want to deny employment to anyone who is capable of doing the work just because he belongs to a visible minority. I believe we all want to see that every person who is impaired physically or mentally has a job. It has been shown that many of these people can do a worth-while job. I do not believe anyone would want to destroy the life of any person because of the colour of their skin when he or she is capable of doing something. However, there is more than one way to skin a cat. I was rather amazed this afternoon listening to Hon. Members of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party opposing this Bill because the legislation is not compulsory. The Hon. Member who just spoke talked about doing something compulsory, that we must tell the employer what he has to do and whom he has to hire. It is not the Canadian way of life for Government to run the businesses of the country. This Government was elected because the people were tired of the Liberal Government trying to run everyone's business and destroying the businesses in that way. Compulsion is not the way of Canadian life. I am happy to see the Hon. Minister bring in a Bill which is not compulsory.
There is another way to do it, the Canadian way, and that is inducement. By inducement we can provide work for those who are in wheelchairs and those who are mentally retarded. I will give you a quick example, Mr. Speaker. There is a school in my home riding of Drumheller because some splendid citizens decided that a number of people who were mentally retarded and some who were physically retarded should not be on welfare. They believed these people could be trained to do things. It would do your heart good, Mr. Speaker, to go to that school and see how these people have made toys and benches. There are some men there of 25 years or 30 years who were formerly on welfare but who are now making a living building things. They showed that they could do it. They were not compelled to do it. It was inducement. I think we can do that throughout this entire country.
Canadian employers are not arrogant. They want to employ those who are handicapped. There has to be some inducement, not compulsion. Would the Hon. Member not agree that the Progressive Conservative way of doing this by inducement is far better than the way of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party of doing it by compulsion?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I wonder how many other of the Hon. Member's colleagues would like to make similar comments because I feel that underscores everything I said about our deep disappointment and betrayed hope. The kind of
conviction that the old Canadian way will do it and so on, is going to leave-
The new Canadian way, not the old.

-one very large proportion of the Canadian population deeply disappointed and convinced that this Government is just making protestations and does not have the guts to follow through. Certainly, where community effort to achieve something exists, it is only to be applauded. I would wonder what kind of employment these people are able to find and what kind of wages they would earn. I trust that they would work their way into jobs which moved them above the poverty line in the Hon. Member's community of Drumheller and I hope very devoutly that occurs. However, I do not believe there is any point in subscribing to the conviction of the good sense of employers as does the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). I believe the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore had a much better sense of where humanity is actually at, and that includes a lot of Canadian employers. There is no particular desire in their hearts to have members of visible minority groups in their workforce. In fact, if those persons were in the workforce complaining about discrimination against them in some aspect or other, including promotions, I dare say, the best thing to do is to keep them out of there. In those various cases, to think that voluntary action will solve the problem is naive, or worse.
In terms of the general sense of being able to get somewhere by depending on voluntary action, I did not suggest that the Government should tell employers who to hire. 1 never suggested anything of the sort in terms of any particular individuals. I do think, as the new Democratic Government in Manitoba has also concluded, that the employment by the Government, and presumably by large employers, should reflect the composition of its workforce. With respect to persons in these four target groups, who probably, in terms of their actual ability to do work, are similar enough to the mainstream white and male population, we can only gain by ensuring that all of those persons are employed. That surely is the basic economic rationale for achieving this social justice policy of employment equity.
The Manitoba Government has carried through something else which is not in this Bill and that is to negotiate arrangements with the provincial Government employees union under which, over a period of time-and it is quite a long period of time, I concede-the employment composition of the Manitoba provincial Government will come to reflect the labour force composition of the province. Therefore, women, aboriginal people, the disabled and visible minority groups will in fact find employment in the Manitoba Government in proportionate numbers to what they exist in the workforce. That kind of provision which was negotiated with the union representing the present employees of the Government of Manitoba-or under the legislation, whatever organization we are dealing with from Government Department to business seeking Government contracts-would ensure that the ability which exists in our society in each of the target areas would in fact find full
October 23, 1985

employment in the Government and an opportunity to exercise there the talents which God gave them. That has to be done, I suggest, by requiring enforceable programs be undertaken by employers and that will ensure they move in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentions what might happen in Manitoba. We will see what the people think about that shortly. However, I can tell the Hon. Member that in Alberta, inducement was used and provided work for not only women, aboriginal people, handicapped and mentally retarded people from Alberta, but from several provinces. Under the Progressive Conservative Government we are using the policy of inducement. The only thing which destroyed it was the National Energy Program brought in by the Liberals, part of which was supported by the New Democratic Party. If I have to tell an employer who invests his money in his now business who he has to hire, I will move to Moscow. We expect compulsion there.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am sorry, the period for questions and comments is now over, enlightening as it may
be.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in connection with Bill C-62, which is an Act respecting employment equity. Unlike the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), I am not disappointed in the least with Bill C-62. In fact, I am very pleased with Bill C-62. Bearing that in mind, and since the Hon. Member seemed to indicate his disappointment when he read Clause 2, the purpose of the Bill, I would just read it myself because I think there is a great deal we can take pleasure from in that clause. It states that:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the work place so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfilment of that goal, to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the same way but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences.
This Bill impacts on four very particular groups: women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities, and persons who, because of race or colour, are part of a visible minority group. When we reflect on that, it is obvious indeed that this Bill will affect the vast majority of people in this country. In fact, it will affect every family in this country. I fail to see how the Hon. Member can be disappointed by a Bill which is going to have such wide implications for in effect virtually every family of every Member of this House. Certainly this Bill will affect my own family. I very much wish that it had been in place some years ago because it would have had a very beneficial effect on one member of my family in particular. I refer to a first cousin of my father's by the name of Ted. Unfortunately, Ted suffered disabilities at birth which affected and impaired his speech and movements throughout his entire life. However, after Ted left school, and with the assistance of a family friend
Employment Equity
who happened to be the Chairman of the City of Toronto Board of Education, he got a job as a custodian in a Toronto school. He worked all of his working days until he retired. In that way he was able to support and look after himself. He was able to make a useful and beneficial contribution not only to himself but to society. It is quite clear that he was able to benefit from having that job, and benefit not only himself but his family and the whole of society. If he had not been fortunate enough to have had some assistance in getting that job, undoubtedly he would have been on social assistance during his lifetime and the taxpayers of this country would have had to have helped support him.
This Bill will make sure that sort of situation will not happen in the future. In the past people like my cousin Ted had to rely on some sort of helping hand, perhaps with political assistance of political friends. That sort of thing is not acceptable today, but if we do not have something to take its place we are going to be in great trouble in this country. Fortunately, what has come along for people like my cousin, people like visible minorities, native people and women, is this Bill on employment equity. How is this Bill going to benefit people like my cousin and others in the position referred to in this Bill? The Bill points out in Clause 4 that employers who are governed by the Canada Labour Relations Code are going to have to identify and eliminate all employment practices which present barriers to the employment of people in those four categories. Not only that, they are going to have to institute positive policies and practices to make sure that we eliminate these barriers. The specific policies, goals and time limits are not spelled out in the Bill in black and white. However, Clause 10 does provide for the Minister to issue guidelines to direct employers pertaining to any of these matters. That is, to set out goals, targets and time limits with respect to hiring, promotion, training and pay practices. All of these things can be covered by the guidelines the Minister will be setting out under Clause 3.
These guidelines will no doubt change from time to time. I have heard criticism in this House today and on other occasions from Members of the Opposition who have indicated that we should have in black and white in this Bill those specific guidelines. They should be set out once and for all, for all time, unchangeable and unchanging. However, all of us know that these things to change from time to time. There is no question that if we looked at employment practices at the turn of this century, they would be different from employment practices in the 1930s. Employment practices in the 1930s would be different from those in the 1950s. Employment practices in the 1950s are different from those today. Therefore, there has to be some flexibility in the Bill and some room to make adjustments which will keep the law current. We have to make sure it applies to present day conditions, which conditions are always changing. We have seen, for example, that a lot of civil rights legislation in other countries has not worked because conditions constantly change. If we sat back and did not make any changes we would have problems and we would be justifiably criticized by the Opposition. On the other hand, if we set

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity
out in the Act the specifics of these goals, targets and time limits, we would find it necessary to make changes through legislation. You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, how difficult it is to make changes in any legislation once it is enacted by this House.
The second aspect of the Bill, then, is the requirement under Clause 5 for employers to prepare and file reports with the Minister. Those reports will outline, of course, what they had been doing in order to eliminate the barriers of discrimination in employment and what new targets and goals they have set forth, as well as time limits within which they accomplish those targets and goals. Clause 5 sets a date of on or before June 1, 1988, for the first of these reports to be filed. We have heard a lot of criticism from our hon. friends in the Opposition about the fact the date was not set sooner than that. The whole process of setting a target date for commencing the filing of reports is to ensure that we give employers a reasonable opportunity to comply and put their plans and policies in place and then to make sure that they are complying with them. From listening to Opposition members talk, one gets the impression that perhaps they are more interested in prosecuting employers and making sure they are hauled before the courts, made an example of, fined, or perhaps even sent to jail. One gets the impression that they are not really interested in seeing the goal of employment equity achieved. That, of course, is really what the Bill is trying to achieve. It is not trying to punish people. It is trying to ensure that Canadian society moves along and that we do attain employment equity. The date and the goals which are set out in the Bill make a lot of sense to most Canadians, if not to the Opposition.
If the reports referred to in the Bill are not filed in the appropriate manner and at the appropriate time, it is an offence under Clause 6 of the Bill which says:
An employer who fails to comply with section 5 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand dollars.
There is that portion of enforcement quite clearly in the Bill which sets out that any employer who fails to report is going to be subject to conviction and to a fine.
