What is going to happen to the reports themselves seems to be the source of a good deal of criticism by my hon. friends in the Opposition. They have indicated that there is no enforcement mechanism in the Bill whatsoever, that these reports will be filed and that will be the end of it. Of course, Mr. Speaker, that is not the case. The Human Rights Commission of Canada is set up to deal with this type of situation. The Human Rights Commission has the ability and authority to either institute proceedings on its own under Section 32.3 of the Human Rights Commission legislation, or to instigate the proceedings on a complaint by any individual who feels that he or she may be aggrieved and that there may be a breach of the intention of this employment equity Bill.
That was the great problem in the past. The average or ordinary citizen has had the ability to lay a complaint and the Commission has had the ability to proceed on its own, but
there has not been evidence available on which to prosecute these complaints and proceed with them. Now, through Bill C-62, there will be this information in the form of reports that will be filed by the Minister and will be available to individuals and employers in order to proceed in laying the complaints and getting results because the evidence will be forthcoming.
The whole employment equity Bill applies to a certain segment of jobs in Canada. It applies, in effect, to all of those jobs that are subject to the Canada Labour Code other than those jobs which are included in the federal civil service and federal Crown corporations. In fact, the total number of jobs to which the Canada Labour Code applies is approximately 1 million. About 500,000, of the jobs will be covered by this Act. Of the other 500,000, 250,000 of the jobs are in the federal civil service itself. There are already, as you know, Mr. Speaker, guidelines, targets and time limits in place for employment equity in the federal civil service. I hope that is taking place. We trust that it is coming to pass. However, if it is not, once again the Human Rights Commission has the right to proceed. Under Section 32.3 of the Act it has the power to initiate complaints.
The same is true of the remaining 250,000 jobs which are in federal Crown corporations. There, too, the Government is issuing guidelines, setting targets and setting time limits. Once again failure to follow through on those goals and objectives will be subject to complaints being laid in front of the Human Rights Commission, either by individuals or on the initiative of the Human Rights Commission itself. Therefore, all of the 1 million jobs that are covered by the Canada Labour Code are going to be subject to this employment equity legislation or to very similar guidelines imposed by the Government itself. There is a mandatory enforcement agency in place which will ensure that employment equity, as outlined in this Bill and in those Government rules and regulations is going to be enforced.
That leaves us with the other group of jobs that is not governed by the Canada Labour Code, those that fall under provincial jurisdiction and are governed by provincial labour codes. With regard to those we have to look to the provinces to implement similar legislation to attain employment equity. There is one other area in which the federal Government can and is getting involved, and that is with employers who have 200 employees or more and have contracts with the federal Government for $200,000 or more. Those employers are also going to be subject to the same guidelines, enforcement provisions and mandatory provisions that are in this Act.
All in all, Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased with this Bill and with the companion approaches that the Government is taking to ensure that there will be employment equity in this country. If I am disappointed at all, it is that the Opposition is not whole-heartedly embracing this Bill and passing it as quickly as possible. I am sure that after hearing the points raised by Government speakers this afternoon we will find that at the end of the debate today all Opposition members will join with us in passing second reading of this Bill right away.

Mr. Speaker, when the time comes to vote on Bill C-62 which we are
October 23, 1985

debating here today, I think it will present a problem for many Members of this House to decide what to do. The purpose of this Bill as indicated in the preamble is very high sounding and the kind of thing that we would all applaud. It says:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the work place so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability-
In other words, aside from the important question of merit, no one should be denied the opportunity to equal access to a position or a job. Another valuable goal of this legislation is to ameliorate the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada. It continues on in the same vein as to its purpose.
I believe that all of us would find great value in the purpose of Bill C-62. Some may say that even though the Bill is not perfect in all its detail, it should be supported because it has some genuine impact on the community. However, the problem arises when one seeks the opinion of those most affected by discrimination. They are most able to know through experience whether such a measure will protect them. That is why I believe we should be hesitant in acting on this legislation. There are those who believe that even though this Bill is inconsequential, it is a slight contribution to our attempt to bring about social justice and, therefore, should be supported. However, there are many organizations interested in employment equity which are denouncing this Bill and saying that it is worse than nothing. Those groups are suggesting that this legislation is so flimsy in its content and ability to achieve moral and legal justice for organizations related to women, the handicapped, native people and visible minorities, that it should be rejected. Such an argument puts a Member of Parliament in a very difficult bind.
It would be unfair and unjust to assume that Members from one side of the House are champions of human rights, equality and social justice. I know that there are individuals from the Conservative benches who have just as much desire to see human rights, justice and equality in the workplace as Members in the opposition. I want to emphasize that it is not acceptable, at this critical moment in our history, to devise a measure that is totally inadequate and only gives lip service to equality. This is not the time to take such action. I hope that Members of the Government as well as the opposition are courageous enough to re-examine this legislation in light of the criticisms made by the visible minority groups, the handicapped groups, native people and women's organization who want to defend their equality rights. We must listen to their concerns.
Those of us who care about human rights have witnessed the long struggle of mankind from the primeval ooze of barbarism and despotism evolve into the faith and democracy in which we live. We are very proud of this country and have seen it evolve over the years through the establishment of commissions to protect the rights of individuals.
Employment Equity
Previous Governments have established a sense of equality not only in terms of language but for all cultures so that they may share equally in this land. Governments have passed legislation that effectively deals with human rights, language equality and the role to be played by multicultural groups. After the struggle to bring the Constitution from England we saw the battle that took place in Parliament to establish a Charter of Rights and Freedoms in that Constitution which would guarantee in law the right of equality before the courts.
The constant struggle upward has been based on the fact that Parliament has had the courage to pass strong laws, regulations and rules that set out the values in our society which must be met. These laws came about as a result of Governments appointing commissions such as the Abella Commission and the Committee on the Disabled. That committee produced the Obstacles Report. That report made recommendations on how the handicapped might overcome the obstacles which were placed before them and left standing by society over the centuries. It was made clear that those obstacles must be eliminated because the time has come to ensure that all people who live in this country will be treated equally by their Governments and society. Those who are unfortunate enough to be handicapped-as could happen to anyone at any time- should continue to enjoy equal opportunity. A committee of the House of Commons was established to study how we would ensure that those who are handicapped and those who do not have these rights would indeed have equality of opportunity and access as well as human rights.
The Abella Commission was established to study the matter of equality in the workplace. It heard from handicapped groups and other organizations about equality in the workplace. It heard from companies and Governments throughout the country about how these people were being treated and if they had equal access. That committee also made its report.
It is the fact that these committees made clear and concise recommendations that we can question whether the Government has read those reports and really responded to them, or is this merely lip service in order to find a compromise with various groups? Is the Government dealing with this issue and acting to bring about fairness in the workplace or is it simply introducing this legislation to get it off the political agenda and show that the Government has taken action? 1 am sure that that is not good enough for the Canadian people and it is certainly not good enough for the people in those four groups we have mentioned.
Women constitute over half of the population of this country. It is not as if we are talking about a small insignificant group which will eventually require attention. Every group is signficant to us in Canada, but certainly when you get a group representing 51 per cent or 52 per cent, it is pretty significant. When you add to the numbers of people involved in that group called women, the native peoples, and you add to that the handicapped and the disabled, then you have a fairly large number of people about whom we are talking. They deserve very serious attention by this Government.

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity
We have worked our way through difficulties throughout these decades. At last we have a report. The Abella Report made it clear what it expected was the sine qua non of an effective policy on this subject. The sine qua non, according to that report, was some kind of teeth, something other than reporting, something other than depending upon public opinion. There has to be in the final analysis a crunch, a bite, a law, a rule, something you can understand and not something that was another step of side-stepping the issue.
It is sad to see the broken promises of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) which are like a broken record. In fact they are a broken record. Once again these broken promises will impact on those less advantaged in our society. They are the ones who will have to wait for social justice.
I was disappointed to hear one member of the Government praise his Government for bringing about such wonderful steps toward social justice since coming into power. The prime basic tool of this Government to deal with society is a budget but the budget gives to the rich and takes from the poor. That cannot be social justice. Here we see that what is important to this Government is rushing to the rescue of banks and large oil companies. It is not rushing to the rescue with meaningful legislation to those who need it most, those who need jobs, those who want to work who are disabled or who want to have equality of salary. It is not fair to the women who were promised by this Prime Minister in the election campaign that they would get equal pay for work of equal value. The Prime Minister also promised that private companies wanting to do business with the Government would have to produce affirmative action plans before they would be awarded contracts.
What happened to those promises made during the election campaign, Mr. Speaker? What have we got? We read in Bill C-62 that after all this labour, effort, groaning and travail that companies need only declare themselves equal opportunity employers to be among those who are eligible for contracts. They make out their own report card. They are for quite some time the judge and the jury of their own abilities. Companies with more than 100 employees who deal with the Government need only sign a document saying they agree to implement some kind of employment equity plan, and there is no definition of what that plan must be in this Bill, at least as I read it. It could be almost anything. This is incredible. In the light of the Abella Commission, it is a joke. I am not laughing, Mr. Speaker, because the Prime Minister is refusing to guarantee that the handicapped, for example, will have better jobs now through a better employment and equity program. If companies can write out their own tickets, and there is no criteria, it seems there is nothing on which to rely for a long time to come. What is more, these reports do not have to be effective until 1988. It does not guarantee to women equal pay for work of equal value.
On March 3, 1984 the Prime Minister in a speech said:
We will ask these firms to show us as part of their tendering responsibilities-
Let me emphasize what he said "to show us"-
-how many women will be hired to fill those contracts. There is nothing alien about that. It is just good sense.
Where is the good sense now, Mr. Speaker? If there is nothing alien about it, why is the Prime Minister alienating those organizations which represent the natives, the handicapped and the women? These organizations are speaking up. If we in the Opposition have to be left to raise our voices on their behalf because the backbenchers in the Tory Party will not do it, then so be it. Let them at least open their eyes and ears to see and hear what these organizations are saying.
Why has the Prime Minister not produced what he promised? The Prime Minister even repeated his promise in Conservative policy papers in the 1984 election campaign during a TV debate, which some of us may remember. He said that private companies doing business with Ottawa will be required to adopt the principle of equal pay for work of equal value. Where is that in this Bill? Where is there equality in the workplace? What an empty thing in a Bill respecting employment equity. Something as fundamental as that promise does not appear.
Under which Minister of the Tory Government does this happen? The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), who was always a staunch and vocal supporter of rights for women, natives and minorities while in Opposition. Where is her strong voice in this situation now, Mr. Speaker? I am sure she can rationalize and feel that she has done her best. I am sure she has done her best in view of some of the comments we have heard in the debates from some of her colleagues. She probably had some stiff opposition. At the same time, that does not solve the problem for the people who belong to these groups. Instead of submitting action plans as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Employment and Immigration promised, companies we are told will be:
-spot checked to determine if these companies are at least beginning to take such basic steps as making up an inventory of their workforce.
Marnie Clarke, Director General of the Employment and Equity Branch of the Department of Employment and Immigration said that. That is bold action, Mr. Speaker. There are going to be spot checks to see if the companies are making up an inventory of their workforce. What a courageous move. Only after three years will more thorough checks be undertaken. After three years, Mr. Speaker, and what does "more thorough checks" really mean? What kind of assurance does this give women, the natives or handicapped? The answer to that is none, Mr. Speaker because this law is not specific. That is why people like Marnie Clarke can talk the way they do. She is not required to lay down any real rules and regulations that will be clear guidelines of what is expected. She says:
We would never stop a contract midway. That would only put people out of work.
That sounds like the approach to South Africa. We do not want to put the blacks out of work in South Africa so, therefore, we will not impose any sanctions. We have heard that argument before. We really will not take any steps against these companies because we do not want to stop them midway
October 23, 1985

through a contract. My goodness, no. That might mean people being thrown out of work. What an amazing way to approach this subject.
I would like to point out one other major concern in this Bill. We are told that the legislation will apply only to companies with more than 100 employees. This winds up including about 100 of 25,000 to 30,000 companies doing business with this Government. That is a very small number of organizations to which this law will apply. It is a lot of noise about nothing.

I was most interested in the Hon. Member's comments, particularly about the crticism levelled against this Bill by a number of groups representing women, visible minorities, disabled and native people. I have heard those criticisms as well but I also know a good many people who fall into those categories; people who are members of some of those organizations. In speaking with them about this subject they said to me "Look, the Liberal Party was in Government for years and years and we did not see anything like this come about, but in less than 12 months with the Progressive Conservative Government we have seen some really significant action and we are very pleased with that significant action and we feel that in fairness we should be giving this legislation a chance to see how it works. We as members of visible minorities, women's groups, native people and disabled are prepared to give this legislation a chance because we think it is good legislation and we know that the Liberal Party and the Liberal Government that was in power for some 20 years did not do anything of this sort".
1 would like to ask the Hon. Member why the Government that he supported and that was in power for some 20 years did not do anything and left it to the current Government to act, just a few months after the Abella Report was tabled? It was tabled in March and the response came in June with the first reading of this Bill. Why, when this Government acted so quickly on the matter of employment equity, was it that his Government did not act in 20 years?

I thank the Hon. Member for his, I think, sincere question. First of all, when he asks about the record of the past Governments, of which I was proud to be a part, I have recited already in my speech a litany of steps that have been taking place throughout decades to move toward human rights and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If he had been in the last House he would have realized how hard we had to fight against the dinosaurs of his Party who were trying to obstruct the Charter of Rights and Freedoms from becoming part of the Constitution.
I would suggest to the Hon. Member that if he sticks around until a little later the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) will be making some comments that will, I think, add to that litany and reply to his question in further detail.
What I would like to come back to in the time allotted to me is a point that the Hon. Member brought up relating to how it
Employment Equity
is that some people who are members of some of these groups that are disadvantaged nonetheless seem to favour this legislation. As I said at the outset of my remarks, many of us are torn as to what to do in terms of voting because, as I said, on the one hand the preamble, the setting out of the purpose, sets forth a very noble purpose. One finds it very heart-rending not to then lend one's support. On the other hand, those organizations that look at this Bill, not the individual members of the group, but those whose business it is in those organizations because they were elected to represent these people, and have studied this, say "This is no good; this is worse than nothing because actually it is toothless and it will give the impression that something is being done when really nothing has been done yet". They are disappointed. I would challenge my hon. friend to please, please seriously look at this and see whether in some way this can be strengthened through amendments, whether this can be looked at in his caucus and explored further in order to give some kind of content to it because these constituent organizations, who are his constituents as well as mine, are saying it is not good enough. They are saying please don't vote for it although they too feel the ultimate purpose is just and desirable.

I would like to address two short questions to the Hon. Member. First of all, it was suggested by the Conservative Member a few moments ago that he has heard from women, handicapped, native people and people who are part of the visible minorities in this country that they like this legislation. I wonder if the Hon. Member would confirm my understanding that the representations made on behalf of all these organizations representing the women's groups, the natives, the handicapped and the visible minorities all make it very clear that they believe that without mandatory provisions, without targets, that this will not work.
The second question I want to ask the Hon. Member is this. Is it not true that under the former Government there were statements of principle endorsing affirmative action and certain specific Departments targetted but in fact very little was accomplished? The number from these disadvantaged groups who actually found employment was very small because again the Departments were not given a target of specific numbers which they should aim to achieve each year.

I thank the Hon. Member for his questions. Certainly I can confirm that all of the major groups which I know relating to women, minority groups and the handicapped and native peoples have in fact condemned this as being inadequate and in most cases hope that we will not pass this because it is just a symbolic gesture and in fact will make some people think that something has been done.
Hon. Members may have seen some of the reports that review all of the organizations that have indicated their displeasure with this, and this has appeared in the media. I urge all Members in this House to look at these reports and at the promises made by the Government before it was elected to see what it said it would do and to see if it could improve on this Bill to include those qualifications which these organizations

feel are a minimum essential in order to reach a level where they could say that we should support it.
In reference to the second part of the question as to whether the last Government failed to adequately deal with the question of equality, as a member in that organization I want to say that, number one, we were engaged in the very long war of attrition to try to bring about a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. To say that it set back our legislative program a year is putting it mildly. Yet I have to confess that despite the fact that that left us in a very difficult hole in terms of getting through other important legislation which was very urgent, it was not enough reason for me to say that I was satisfied that we did all we should have done. I think if we as Members were prepared as Hon. Members from time to time to admit that we could do better or that we could have done better, it would be better for this House and especially for the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Eglington-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) said he liked legislation with teeth. I believe him. His Party certainly brought in legislation with teeth. For example, the national energy policy. It had teeth. It destroyed, masticated an entire industry in Alberta. It threw hundreds of women, native people, handicapped people and people from other countries out of work. It destroyed the hopes of a province. It was designed to destroy a province. Yes, I can believe that the Hon. Member wants legislation with teeth.
With the Hon. Member's record and the record of his Government which he supported when it brought in the national energy policy, I marvel that he now talks about equality. I wish he had talked about equality before he destroyed an industry in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak in this debate today in support of Bill C-62. I believe this is a Bill that is progressive in nature and I am very pleased to be part of a Government that has brought forth this progressive legislation.
Employment equity in this country is long overdue. With more and more women and minorities entering the labour force the need for equal employment opportunity has increased rapidly. In the next decade, as many as 70 per cent of all new workers in Canada will be women, native people and people with physical handicaps.
As the birth rate and the number of immigrant workers declines, employers will have to turn to women and other minorities. Canadian businesses simply cannot afford to ignore such a vast pool of talent and ability. As a vice president of a large corporation said, in the decades ahead, any organization that ignores or underestimates the potential of women or overlooks any source of talent for that matter will be making a fatal mistake. No truer words have ever been spoken.
By eliminating barriers to equal opportunity in policy, training programs, pay scales and company practices, employees will be better motivated and more productive. Employment
equity will increase productivity, reduce the high job turnover that now exists and eliminate dead-end jobs.
The Bill that is before Parliament today represents a practical and reasonable approach to employment equity. Its purpose is to encourage equality in employment by eliminating barriers to hiring, promotion, salaries and many other areas. All federally regulated companies with over 100 employees and any private firm that tenders on Government contracts worth over $200,000 will be subject to the measures contained in this Bill. Under this criteria, Bill C-62 affects not only all Crown corporations and federal agencies but 500 private government suppliers as well.
Employers will be required to identify and remove barriers to equal employment opportunity. Annual reports providing a detailed breakdown of the labour force by designated groups will also be required. These reports will give a listing of occupations within the employer's business showing where designated group members are represented. They will also show salary ranges, hirings, promotions and terminations of designated group members relative to the employer's total number of employees. Employers who fail to report will be subject to a fine.
We on this side of the House believe that this is the kind of workable approach to employment equity that Canadians want. Forcing companies to maintain quotas or subscribe to unmanageable guidelines in order to comply with Government regulations is not the way to promote employment equity. Instead, the Government must create a positive, constructive atmosphere to change. This cannot be done by enforcing quotas but by setting workable goals and attainable targets.
Business leaders must be awakened to the potential of all participants in the labour force. They need to see that by denying one segment of a society a role in their companies, they are damaging their own economic interests and the economic interests of Canada as a whole. Changes in attitude will take place but they will take place slowly.
In the past decade, many progressive steps have been taken. Let me cite a few. Since 1969, at least as many women as men have entered management positions in the Government. There are four times as many women attending professional schools now than there were in 1971.
A recent survey conducted by the Harvard Business Review found that attitudes toward and about women in businesses have changed dramatically in the past 20 years. In 1965, for example, one-half of the man and women surveyed agreed that women rarely expected or wanted positions of authority. Today, fewer than 10 per cent believe this to be true. In 1961, 61 per cent of the men surveyed believed that the business community would never wholly accept women. Today, that figure stands at 20 per cent. Perhaps the most notable quote that came from this survey came from a woman who said, "The biggest factor in the acceptance of women executives is the simple passage of time and the passing of the old boys in the good old boys network''.
October 23, 1985

Members opposite do not believe that voluntary or nonquota employment equity legislation can work. Let me provide the House with an example of an outstanding affirmative action program for women. A company located in my riding of Scarborough Centre has had an affirmative action program in place for 10 years. In 1975, 10 years ago, Warner-Lambert, a large pharmaceutical and confectionery company in Scarborough employing nearly 2,000 people, initiated a formal affirmative action program for women with the following central objective:
To assess the current status of women at Warner-Lambert... to recommend the most effective ways to remedy any existing negatives found in our policies, practices and attitudes, respecting employment or promotion opportunities for female employees.
This is a program that was set up 10 years ago without legislation. The company established a volunteer committee. The only criteria for joining this committee was an interest and a willingness to serve. The committee examined seven key issues: job access, compensation, employee benefits, the company policy manual, maternity leave, day care and communications. The success of this program has been remarkable. Female representation in management positions has increased by 202 per cent. Women now represent 34 per cent of the company's supervisory management group compared to 18 per cent in 1975. Application forms were redrawn to remove old biases. Annual studies are now done to guarantee fairness of compensation levels. Specific benefit plan clauses which were discriminatory have been removed. The company policy was rewritten and a counselling service for employees who are mothers-to-be was established. Female turnover in this company has been reduced by 20 per cent and recruitment and orientation costs are lower because more vacancies are filled from within.
Warner-Lambert represents a successful, voluntary approach to employment equity. Its program for women was not established as a response to pressure from special interest groups or government regulation but from a sincere desire to better the conditions of its workers and to obtain the maximum input possible from all its employees. This is the type of positive, constructive approach this Government wants to initiate in the private sector. I am proud that this particular company which I have cited is in the riding of Scarborough Centre.
Employment equity will come to Canada. However, it will come not from quotas or restrictive legislation; it will come from the type of enlightened programs such as those at Warner-Lambert and the progressive legislation of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald).
Hear, hear!

Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
Employment Equity

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. I think we all join in praising and congratulating any company which voluntarily implements a policy to increase the number of people employed and the responsibility of the positions which they hold from groups which have traditionally not been able to obtain those types of jobs. I wish to ask the Hon. Member whether or not she is aware of the fact that studies conducted by Government and organizations such as the organization respecting the status of women have clearly indicated that despite everything being done the percentage of women who hold executive positions is still very small. Is she aware that even for those who hold executive positions the income they earn is substantially lower by thousands of dollars than that earned by men holding similar positions?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member's question. As the Vice-Chairman of the Equality Rights Committee, which will be reporting to the House this week, we had the opportunity to travel across Canada to listen to groups. Of course, the National Action Committee made representation in nearly every city across the country. We heard of the need for opportunities, the need for employment equity and the need to implement the Abella Report. What I believe we have in Canada is an awareness to the point that what we need is not quotas, which I believe the Hon. Member and his Party recommend, but opportunities. We know that in order to achieve equity between men and women we need financial equity. However, in order to achieve financial equity we have to have opportunities. I am speaking of opportunities in the workplace-the opportunities for jobs. The fact that over one million people are unemployed does not help women. What we need is a buoyant economy. That is what will help women.
There are a number of other provisions which need to be put in place. I would like to refer to the need for child care and family care with respect to the question of employment equity and employment opportunities for women. As I understand it, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) will be setting up a task force shortly which will be dealing with the question of child care. The setting up of that task force, along with establishing opportunities, will provide a big boost for women in order to achieve the type of equity which is so long overdue. I have been waiting for it in Scarborough, as have women all across the country. We have been waiting for the federal Government to bring forward some type of legislation. Here we are in 1985, 10 years after Warner-Lambert started its programs, finally at a point at which we are bringing forward this type of legislation which I believe is extremely progressive. I am pleased to support it.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member suggests the way to overcome the tremendous difficulties which various minority groups have faced in achieving employment is to have a buoyant economy. I remind the Hon. Member that from 1945 to approximately 1960 we had virtually full employment in the country. However, the target groups including women,

October 23, 1985
Employment Equity
handicapped and the visible minorities, did not obtain jobs even though there was full employment.
It seems that the Hon. Member and so many of her colleagues on the Government side have endorsed the idea that we must not have compulsion. They believe that we must do these things through voluntary actions. I wish to remind the Hon. Member that in the 1940s and the 1950s when it became apparent across the country that certain groups were not welcome in certain jobs or in certain hotels and restaurants that the Governments, federal and provincial, brought in legislation with respect to fair employment and fair accommodation practices. In this respect I give credit to the Ontario Conservative Government of the day which brought in the first legislation with respect to fair employment and fair accommodation practices. The Conservative Government of Ontario brought in that legislation because it realized that appealing to the goodwill of those who were discriminating would not work. I ask the Hon. Member why she is now adopting an approach which the Conservative Government of many years ago found did not work. Why is she rejecting that experience and the policies of the Conservative Government of Ontario which it adopted with respect to the concept of voluntary action bringing about real change?
Mr. Speaker, it is curious that the Hon. Member would compare 1985 to 1945.
It is not much different!

It is a completely different situation today. As we will recall, veterans came home from the war in 1945 when there was a completely different type of mentality. Women were so pleased to have the men home that they were willing to give up jobs. The same holds true with respect to the conclusion of the First World War. We obtained the vote in 1917. What happened after that? The war was over and women went back to looking after their children, their homes and so on. It was the same type of situation in 1945. However, in 1985, we find ourselves in a different situation. Since the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in 1971, there has been a real awakening within the country that employment equity is here to stay.
Since the Hon. Member brought up the hotel business, I would like to tell him what the Personnel Director of the Westin Bayshore Hotel in Vancouver who employs 500 people said:
Affirmative action is not the monster we thought it was going to be ... Once set up, the program doesn't take much time to operate-
I think voluntary employment equity is exactly what we need. It is a progressive move.
